approved: Australian Securities and Investments Commission Amendment (Corporations and Markets Advisory Committee Abolition) Bill 2014

Ed Husic Earlier in the debate on this bill, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission Amendment (Corporations and Markets Advisory Committee Abolition) Bill 2014, I was reflecting on the great work that CAMAC has done, particularly in trying to work out a framework for the introduction of crowdsourced equity funding in Australia, and what that might do to help support businesses, particularly start-ups and those that are at the early stage of innovation, being able to get access to much-needed capital. As I indicated earlier, CAMAC brought down a very comprehensive report in May. I would like to congratulate the subcommittee of CAMAC who brought that report down, led by chair, Greg Vickery AO, from Norton Rose Australia; along with Teresa Handicott from Corrs Chambers Westgarth; Professor Ian Ramsay, who is a professor of commercial law at the University of Melbourne; and Brian Salter, who is the General Counsel at AMP; and they were assisted by ASIC's Maan Beydoun. Even in mentioning those names, you get a sense of the calibre of people who have committed to assist in CAMAC's work. As I indicated in my earlier contribution, from a policy perspective it is simply a tragedy that with the abolition of CAMAC we will lose those skills and that expertise, and the acquisition of the insights of that body—and it is assumed that, once CAMAC is demolished in the way that is proposed, the three people currently working for CAMAC will be absorbed by Treasury. It is an absolute tragedy that the government will have to pay more to get that expertise, as opposed to what they had at hand and the great work CAMAC has done, such as this report. This report on crowdsource equity funding was widely welcomed by many for its breadth. It looked at jurisdictions—particularly in the US, the UK, New Zealand, Canada and within the EU—that are working very hard to put, or have put, in place mechanisms to allow crowdsource equity funding. Supported abolishing the Corporations and Markets Advisory Committee as one of 36 government bodies being scrapped to save an estimated $500 million over the forward estimates, cited Australia's ranking of 124 out of 148 countries for regulatory burden, and said Labor had introduced more than 21,000 additional regulations in five and a half years.

Opposed the bill abolishing the Corporations and Markets Advisory Committee, pointing to the government's earlier backdowns on abolishing the Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission and the Independent National Security Legislation Monitor as evidence of poor judgement, and quoted Professor Ian Ramsay's description of the cut as saving only three salaries.

Supported the bill abolishing the Corporations and Markets Advisory Committee, projected to save $2.8 million over the forward estimates, said the government has reduced the number of government bodies by more than 250 since the 2013 election, and reported a net reduction of more than $2.1 billion in compliance costs from its deregulation agenda.

Opposed the abolition of the Corporations and Markets Advisory Committee, praising its May report on crowdsourced equity funding, and said Labor's December position paper called for investor safeguards, easier start-up access to crowdsourced funding, and priority legislation, urging the government to proceed with the reforms while reconsidering scrapping the committee.

Supported abolishing the Corporations and Markets Advisory Committee as part of a smaller government agenda, citing $2.8 million in savings over the forward estimates, and said the government is borrowing over $1 billion each month to service Labor's debt, framing every saving as important to budget repair.

Opposed abolishing the Corporations and Markets Advisory Committee, tracing its independent advisory role to 1978, and cited submissions from the Australian Institute of Company Directors, the Law Council of Australia and other bodies opposing the move, noting the committee has operated for less than $1 million a year since 1998 while delivering highly valued corporate law reform advice.

Closed debate on the bill to abolish the Corporations and Markets Advisory Committee, saying the government inherited 1,252 separate government bodies from Labor and has already reduced the number by 251, citing the $5.7 billion Medibank Private sale and combined smaller government savings expected to total $539.5 million.
